vignette:
The Weight of Locked Doors

Maria is fifty-nine years old, a project manager for a mid-sized construction firm in Houston, and she moves through her days with the kind of controlled precision that colleagues mistake for confidence. She arrives early, leaves late, and keeps her calendar color-coded down to fifteen-minute intervals. What her colleagues do not see is that she plans her routes to every meeting in advance, identifies every exit before she sits down, and has not slept more than three consecutive hours in longer than she can remember.

Eleven years ago, Maria was traveling for work in her home country of Colombia, conducting site visits for a development project near Medellín. On a Tuesday morning in October, she was taken from her vehicle at a roadblock by armed men. She was held for twenty-three days in a series of structures — a shed, a basement, a room with no windows — bound, blindfolded for long stretches, and subjected to repeated interrogations that turned violent. She did not know, from one hour to the next, whether she would be released or killed. She was eventually freed following negotiations she was never fully told about, flown back to Houston, and told by well-meaning family members that the important thing was that she was safe now.

She was not safe. She simply was no longer there.

The first years after her return were, by her own description, a kind of performance. She went back to work within six weeks because stillness was unbearable. She finalized her divorce — a marriage that had already been fracturing — and threw herself into managing projects, timelines, and people, because control over external systems was the only thing that quieted the noise inside. She told almost no one what had happened. Her children knew she had been "in a difficult situation." Her mother knew she had been hurt. No one knew the details, and she preferred it that way.

What she cannot control is what happens at night. She wakes in a cold sweat, certain she can smell the damp concrete of the basement, certain there is someone standing at the edge of her bed. She lies rigid until her eyes adjust to the darkness of her own bedroom, and then she gets up, turns on every light in the apartment, and sits at her kitchen table until dawn. She has done this so many times that she has stopped trying to go back to sleep. She drinks coffee and reviews project schedules instead.

During the day, certain things ambush her without warning. The sound of a deadbolt sliding home — in an office bathroom, in a restaurant — sends a spike of terror through her chest that she has learned to absorb without visible reaction. A man raising his voice in a meeting can pull her out of the present so completely that she loses minutes at a time, returning to herself to find her pen has torn through the paper of her notepad. She is hypervigilant in a way that exhausts her: scanning parking garages, refusing to sit with her back to a door, monitoring the body language of strangers with an intensity that she knows is not rational and cannot stop.

She describes a persistent feeling of being hollow — of watching her own life from a slight distance, as though she is a very competent understudy playing a role written for someone else. She loves her adult children but finds that she cannot fully feel that love in the moments when she is with them. She laughs at the right times. She brings the right gifts. She notices the gap between the gesture and the feeling and grieves it quietly.

What brought her to therapy, finally, was a routine fire drill at her office. The alarm, the locked stairwell doors propped open, the stream of people moving in one direction — she found herself on the sidewalk outside with no memory of how she got there, shaking so hard she had to sit on the curb. A younger colleague crouched beside her and asked if she was all right. She said yes. She was not.
